land.text: the Tuyuhun lands around Qinghai Lake, which the Tibetan Empire page says 'was defeated by the Tibetan army and gradually assimilated into Tibetan culture' (663)

successors.note: The Tuyuhun page's infobox says 'Destroyed by the Tibetan Empire: 670' and the Battle of Dafeichuan page says the Tibetans conquered Tuyuhun in 669; the Tibetan Empire page lists the defeat under 663 and has Gar Tongtsen 'after having incorporated Tuyuhun into Tibetan territory' die in 667, which fits 663. The Tuyuhun court (Murong Nuohebo, reign to 672 on the page) lived on in exile.

capitals.name: Fuqi (Tiebujia ruins, Gonghe, Qinghai)
capitals.note: The infobox gives 'Fuqi (in modern Gonghe, Qinghai)' as the capital and the text says it 'was moved 6 kilometres (3.7 mi) west of Qinghai Lake' without a year; the page does not date the capital for any span, so Fuqi is drawn for the whole life. Coordinates approximate (a site west of Qinghai Lake). Fuqi appears on the page as the single capital, no other seat is named.

rulers.name: Murong Tuyuhun
rulers.title: Henan King
rulers.note: Reign years from the rulers table of the Tuyuhun page; the page says he died 'in Linxia, Gansu' in 317.

rulers.name: Murong Shuluogan
rulers.title: Wuyin Khan / Da Chanyu / Wu King

rulers.name: Murong Fuyun
rulers.title: Busabo Khan
rulers.note: Murong Fuyun page: made khan in 597 after Shifu's assassination; died fleeing the Tang in 635. Driven out by the Sui in 608-609 and restored under Tang Gaozu.

rulers.name: Murong Shun
rulers.title: Prince of Xiping / Gandou Khan
rulers.note: Briefly khan in 609 under the Sui; surrendered to Li Jing in 635 and was made Prince of Xiping and Zhugulüwugandou Khan.

rulers.name: Murong Nuohebo
rulers.title: Wudiyebaledou Khan
rulers.note: Reign 635-672 on the Tuyuhun page; the kingdom itself is gone from 663 in this dossier (court in exile after the Tibetan conquest).

correction.text: unchanged Qinghai Lake / Qaidam / Hexi-edge shape, drawn from 284 instead of 287: 'The Tuyuhun Empire was established in 284 by subjugating the native peoples referred to as the Qiang'

keyframe_review.note: Years only: Cliopatria starts in 287, the Tuyuhun page's infobox and text say 284. The page is not consistent with itself (Murong groups reach 'the pasture lands around Qinghai Lake about the middle of the 3rd century'; Murong Shegui's group crosses the Yellow River 307-313 into eastern Qinghai); the 284 founding is the page's own. The page names no border, so the 279,362 km2 shape (bbox 88.7-103.0 E, 35.6-39.5 N, whose east edge sits just short of Linxia, where Tuyuhun died in 317) stands, soft.
279,338 km2: identical to 287 within vertex noise (0.01%); no page opened gives a border change for 306.
279,264 km2, vertex noise again; the page's only dated move in this decade is Murong Shegui's group crossing the Yellow River between 307 and 313 into eastern Qinghai (no land change recorded).
279,338 km2 for 324-386: a 63-year span in which the page records no territorial event (rulers Yeyan, Suixi, Shilian). Unverified in detail: page budget.
278,443 km2: the east edge moves 0.08 degrees (vertex noise); no page dates a change in 387.
278,493 km2, vertex noise; no change recorded.
278,444 km2, vertex noise; no change recorded.

278,518 km2 for 414-425. The Western Qin page has Qifu Chipan 'launch[ing] several campaigns against the Tuyuhun' after 414 and a Tuyuhun and Qiang population rebelling inside Western Qin (421-428), without a border change; the shape stands.

correction.text: the 426 shape (316,763 km2, reaching 34.2 N and 103.7 E) drawn from 430, not 426; 426-429 keep the 414 shape: 'the rest of Qin's territory was conquered by the Tuyuhun, leaving Mumo with only a lone city'

keyframe_review.note: Years only: the Western Qin page dates the Tuyuhun conquest of what was left of Western Qin to 430 (Helian Ding then forced Qifu Mumo to stop at Nan'an; he surrendered in 431), where Cliopatria's expansion starts in 426 (Chipan's 'worst defeat' of 426 is Xia's and Liang's doing, not Tuyuhun's). Cliopatria keeps a Western Qin shape of 199,463 km2 to 438, which is wrong for 431-438.

344,663 km2: the south edge drops from 34.2 N to 32.75 N (+28,000 km2, northern Sichuan side). No page opened dates or explains this move; the Tuyuhun page lists 'northern Sichuan' in the empire's extent. Recorded as a confidence-1 gain from nobody (Qiang tribes).
344,539 km2, identical to 439 within noise; 441-468.

393,822 km2: the west edge moves from 88.7 E to 85.1 E (+49,000 km2, the Qaidam's west and the Altun side). No page dates it; the Shanshan page says only that 'from the 5th century onwards ... the land was frequently invaded by nomads such as Tuyuhuns, the Rourans'. Confidence-1 gain.

554,385 km2 (bbox 81.7-103.7 E, 32.75-41.07 N, about 1,900 x 920 km at these latitudes), 476-535. Page sanity check: the Tuyuhun page gives 'stretching 1,500 kilometres from east to west and 1,000 kilometres from north to south' and an extent of 'Qinghai, Gansu, Ningxia, northern Sichuan, eastern Shaanxi, southern Xinjiang, and most of Tibet'. The infobox has no area; a 1.5 x 1.0 thousand km box (1.5 M km2) is not an area, so no ratio is claimed. Ningxia, eastern Shaanxi and 'most of Tibet' lie outside this shape; the page names no frontier there, so the shape stands and the claim goes to notes. Growth to the Tarim rim (Lop Nur, Charklik) is not dated by any page opened.
554,557 km2 for 536-586; no change in area. Page: Songyun visited 'in 518' (no border). Unverified: page budget.
554,703 km2 for 587-601, the vertex count rises (97 to 118) without an area change. The Northern Zhou page opened for this period is silent on Tuyuhun.

correction.text: unchanged shape for 602-607 and again from 619; in between the land is the Sui's: 'Emperor Yang had his forces seize Tuyuhun's territory, establishing four commanderies' (608), and 'Under Emperor Gaozu of Tang, Fuyun recovered the Tuyuhun lands'

keyframe_review.note: Cliopatria draws the Tuyuhun whole through 627, but the Sui seized its territory in 608 and divided it into four commanderies; Fuyun returned in 609 and was driven out again; he recovered the lands only under Tang Gaozu (618-626; the Murong Fuyun page gives no year, so 619 is a bridging judgment). The loss (608) and gain (619) are in the ledger on top of this baseline shape; Fuyun's refuge is 'the mountains' to the southwest.
554,277 km2, vertex noise. Fuyun raids Tang prefectures from 622 and Tang envoys are detained before 634; no land changes hands.
554,131 km2 for the single year 633; no change.

553,602 km2 for 634-637. Fall 634: Tang armies attack and Tuyuhun raids Liang Prefecture (Wuwei); summer 635: Li Jing defeats Fuyun, who dies fleeing, and Murong Shun surrenders and is made Prince of Xiping and khan. The Tuyuhun infobox gives 'Vassal of the Tang dynasty: 634' and the Tibetan Empire page has Songtsen Gampo defeating the Tuyuhun in 634; the Tang vassal tint is recorded in tang-dynasty.json. The area does not change.

516,020 km2: the south edge rises from 32.75 N to 34.68 N (-37,600 km2). The Tuyuhun page says 'the Tuyuhun Empire lost much of its territory in southern Gansu to Tibetans' after the Tibetan attack, without a year and naming Gansu rather than southern Qinghai; recorded as a confidence-1 loss to the Tibetan Empire in 638.

355,398 km2: the west edge returns to 85.1 E and the north edge to 39.5 N (-160,600 km2, the Tarim rim). No page opened says who took it or when. Recorded as a confidence-1 loss with counterpart 'nobody' as a placeholder; a gap-filler should open the Anxi Protectorate and Qiemo pages.

correction.text: unchanged shape, ending in 663 instead of 665: the Tibetan Empire page lists the Tuyuhun/Azha kingdom as 'defeated by the Tibetan army' in 663

keyframe_review.note: Years only. The pages disagree: Tibetan Empire 663 (and 'after having incorporated Tuyuhun into Tibetan territory, ... Gar Tongtsen died in 667'); Battle of Dafeichuan 'In 669, the Tibetan Empire invaded and conquered the Tuyuhun kingdom of Qinghai'; Tuyuhun infobox 'Destroyed by the Tibetan Empire: 670'. Cliopatria ends in 665. 663 is used because the 667 sentence rules out the later dates. 355,400 km2.

region.text: the Cliopatria 287 shape (Qinghai Lake, Qaidam and the Hexi edge), drawn from 284 as the keyframe tuyuhun_287 does: 'The Tuyuhun Empire was established in 284 by subjugating the native peoples referred to as the Qiang'

ledger.note: 284: the Murong Xianbei found the Tuyuhun at Qinghai Lake. 'The Tuyuhun Empire was established in 284 by subjugating the native peoples referred to as the Qiang'; infobox 'Established: 284'. The page also has Murong Shegui's group crossing the Yellow River in 307-313 into eastern Qinghai, and Cliopatria starts in 287; the core is the Cliopatria 287 shape near Qinghai Lake. Revised by fx-41 (window request R033): the region was the Cliopatria 287 shape cut to 250 km round Xining (331 cells), so the ledger drew 331 cells in 284-286 and the keyframe snapped 786 cells in 287; the keyframe tuyuhun_287 now carries from 284, and this event founds the state on the same shape so that no snap is needed. The Tuyuhun page (re-read 2 Nov 2026) gives 'established in 284' and no extent for the first years, so the 279,362 km2 outline stays soft.

region.text: the rest of Western Qin's territory in southern Gansu (Cliopatria's 426 expansion, 316,763 km2 against 278,518 km2)

ledger.note: 430: the Tuyuhun take what is left of Western Qin. 'Meanwhile, the rest of Qin's territory was conquered by the Tuyuhun, leaving Mumo with only a lone city'; Xia ends Western Qin at Nan'an in 431. The page dates the sentence to 430 by its narrative; Cliopatria starts this expansion in 426. The Northern Wei page adds: 'In 431, the last Xia emperor, Helian Ding was captured and handed over to Wei by the Tuyuhun.'

region.text: the southward extension of the 439 shape from 34.2 N to 32.75 N (about 28,000 km2)

ledger.note: 439: the Tuyuhun spread south into the Qiang country (northern Sichuan side). Page silent on the date: the Tuyuhun page lists 'northern Sichuan' in the extent but dates nothing here; the year is Cliopatria's.

region.text: the Qaidam's west edge from 88.7 E to 85.1 E (about 49,000 km2)

ledger.note: 469: the Tuyuhun reach west toward the Altun. Page silent on the date: the Shanshan page says only 'From the 5th century onwards ... the land was frequently invaded by nomads such as Tuyuhuns, the Rourans'; the year is Cliopatria's.

region.text: the south Tarim and Lop Nur rim to 81.7 E and 41.07 N (about 160,000 km2)

ledger.note: 476: the Tuyuhun hold the Charklik and Qiemo country. Page silent on the date: the Shanshan page has Shanshan 'ruled from Qiemo' after Juqu Anzhou's invasion of Loulan in 442 and the Tuyuhuns among the later invaders; the year is Cliopatria's.

region.text: Tuyuhun's territory, 'seize[d]' by the Sui and divided into 'four commanderies, to be populated with exiles'

ledger.note: 608: the Sui seize the Tuyuhun lands. 'In 608 as well, Pei Ju persuaded the Tiele tribes to attack Tuyuhun, forcing Tuyuhun's Busabuo Khan Murong Fuyun to flee'; 'Emperor Yang had his forces seize Tuyuhun's territory, establishing four commanderies'. The Murong Fuyun page adds that Fuyun fled to Xiping and then 'southwest into the mountains', returned in 609 and was driven out again; Yang toured the 'newly conquered Tuyuhun territory' in spring 609.

region.text: the lands of the Tuyuhun, which 'Fuyun recovered' under Tang Gaozu

ledger.note: 619: Fuyun regains the Tuyuhun lands as the Sui falls. Page silent on the year: 'Under Emperor Gaozu of Tang, Fuyun recovered the Tuyuhun lands and agreed to attack Li Gui'; the Fuyun page has Yang killed at Jiangdu in 619, and Fuyun raiding Tang prefectures from 622, so the lands were back by then.

region.text: Shan Prefecture (Haidong), Lan and Kuo prefectures and Liang Prefecture (Wuwei), raided by the Tuyuhun, and the grasslands to the west where Li Jing pursued Fuyun

ledger.note: 634: the Tang-Tuyuhun war begins. 'Fall 634: Duan Zhixuan and Fan Xing attacked, but Tuyuhun forces avoided combat. Tuyuhun then raided Liang Prefecture (modern Wuwei, Gansu)'; the Tuyuhun page has Songtsen Gampo defeating the Tuyuhun 'near Qinghai Lake' the same year.

region.text: the war zone between Liang Prefecture and Qinghai Lake

ledger.note: 635: Li Jing defeats the Tuyuhun. 'Summer 635: Li Jing's forces engaged Tuyuhun, and Fuyun burned the grasslands and fled'; the nobles led by Murong Shun surrendered and Fuyun died fleeing. Taizong made Shun Prince of Xiping and khan: the Tuyuhun become a Tang vassal (infobox 'Vassal of the Tang dynasty: 634'; the tint is in tang-dynasty.json).

region.text: the southern edge from 32.75 N to 34.68 N, 'southern Gansu' in the page's words

ledger.note: 638: the Tuyuhun lose their south to Tibet. Page: 'Although the Tibetans withdrew in response, the Tuyuhun Empire lost much of its territory in southern Gansu to Tibetans.' The page gives no year; the year is Cliopatria's, and the page's 'southern Gansu' is not the same place as Cliopatria's cut, which is southern Qinghai (Yushu side).

region.text: the Tarim rim and the north edge from 41.07 N to 39.5 N and the west edge from 81.7 E to 85.1 E (about 160,000 km2)

ledger.note: 641: the Tuyuhun lose the Tarim rim. Page silent on who took it and when; Cliopatria's 641 shape drops it. 'nobody' is a placeholder for an unknown taker, not a statement that the land was stateless.

region.text: the Tuyuhun lands around Qinghai Lake, taken by the Tibetan Empire

ledger.note: 663: the Tibetan army defeats the Tuyuhun. The Tibetan Empire page: the Tuyuhun/Azha kingdom 'was defeated by the Tibetan army and gradually assimilated into Tibetan culture' (663); the Tuyuhun infobox says 670 and the Dafeichuan page 669. The Tang try to restore the kingdom and lose at Dafeichuan in 670.

wars.name: Tuyuhun conquest of the rest of Western Qin
wars.outcome: The Tuyuhun conquered what was left of Western Qin in 430, leaving Qifu Mumo one city; Xia ended Western Qin at Nan'an in 431, and the Tuyuhun captured Helian Ding of Xia and handed him to Northern Wei in 431.
wars.note: Second page for the Helian Ding sentence: Northern Wei.

wars.name: Sui conquest of Tuyuhun
wars.outcome: Tiele attack and Sui occupation in 608 force Fuyun to flee; Fuyun returns in 609 and is driven out again by Emperor Yang in person; the land is held as four commanderies until the Sui collapse.
wars.note: The Murong Fuyun page adds Western Tujue attacks on the Tuyuhun in 613 and the recovery under Tang Gaozu.

wars.name: Tang campaign against Tuyuhun

zones.text: Shan, Lan, Kuo and Liang prefectures to Qinghai Lake

wars.outcome: Li Jing defeats Fuyun in summer 635; Murong Shun is made Prince of Xiping and khan; the Tuyuhun become a Tang vassal without losing land.
wars.note: The Tuyuhun page has Taizong defeating the 'Tibetan army' in 635-636 as well; the Tibetan Empire page says 'the Emperor attacked and defeated the Tuyuhun' in 635-636.

wars.name: Tibetan conquest of Tuyuhun

zones.text: Qinghai Lake and the Tuyuhun lands

wars.outcome: Songtsen Gampo defeats the Tuyuhun near Qinghai Lake in 634; the Tibetans take southern territory soon after; the kingdom is defeated in 663 (other pages: 669, 670).
wars.note: A long war in two moves (634, 663); the Tuyuhun page's wording for the middle years: 'the Tuyuhun Empire lost much of its territory in southern Gansu to Tibetans'.

wars.name: Battle of Dafeichuan
wars.outcome: Tibetan pyrrhic victory: Xue Rengui's Tang army sent to restore the Tuyuhun retreats; the Tuyuhun are not restored and the Tibetan Empire holds their land.
wars.note: Fought after the Tuyuhun kingdom had ended in this dossier (663); no border of the Tuyuhun moves.

certainty.note: Highland and steppe frontiers throughout; no page opened gives a treaty or survey line for the Tuyuhun. The Sui commanderies of 608 are administrative units but their extent is not given.

notes:
Cliopatria shape rows: 22 shapes, all reviewed. Most differences between consecutive shapes are vertex noise (area change below 0.5 percent); the real steps are 426 (+37,000 km2), 439 (+28,000), 469 (+49,000), 476 (+160,000), 638 (-37,600) and 641 (-160,600). Of these only 426 (Western Qin, 430) is dated by a page I opened. 439, 469, 476, 638 and 641 are confidence-1 ledger events: the pages are silent on year and on who lost or gained (counterpart 'nobody' for 439, 469 and 641 is a placeholder; 476 names Shanshan from the Shanshan page's own wording). A gap-filler should open the Northern Liang, Rouran Khaganate, Qiemo, Anxi Protectorate, Dangxiang and 'Tang-Tibetan' pages for the Tarim rim, the 5th-century Qaidam and the 638-641 moves.
Disagreements between pages for the end of the state: Tibetan Empire 663 (used), Battle of Dafeichuan 669, Tuyuhun infobox 670, Cliopatria 665. The Tuyuhun court continued in exile under Murong Nuohebo to 672 (rulers table); it held no territory in this dossier after 663.
The Tuyuhun page claims an extent of 'Qinghai, Gansu, Ningxia, northern Sichuan, eastern Shaanxi, southern Xinjiang, and most of Tibet', 1,500 x 1,000 km. Cliopatria's shape (555,000 km2 at most) leaves out Ningxia, eastern Shaanxi and most of Tibet. The page names no frontier or date for any of it, so the shape is not changed; flagged for a reviewer who has a better source (Seshat cn_tuyuhun was not opened).
Vassalage: the Tuyuhun page's infobox says 'Vassal of the Tang dynasty: 634'; the vassal tint belongs to tang-dynasty.json (vassal_start with counterpart tuyuhun). No vassal event is written here because in the schema 'this state' is the suzerain.
The 608-619 Tuyuhun-Sui interval is drawn through loss (608) and gain (619, a bridging year) over the baseline 602 shape, not through a separate keyframe.
Capital coordinates (Fuqi, a site west of Qinghai Lake) are approximate; the page gives only 'in modern Gonghe, Qinghai' and '6 kilometres west of Qinghai Lake'. The gazetteer has no 'Gonghe' or 'Fuqi'; the region 'Qinghai (region)' and the lake 'Qinghai' do exist.
Names for the gazetteer: none new beyond the use of 'Xining', 'Wuwei' (both places), 'Qinghai (region)'.
Counterparts needing dossiers: Shanshan (kingdom of Loulan/Qiemo), Tiele tribes (minor). 'xia' and 'western-qin' are owned by ea-03 parts; the Tuyuhun is the counterpart of their losses.
